Recently a colleague of mine shown us a demo using a fresh model designing a building construction detail live, in minutes, which is a function that we struggled to bring into our construction design software due to resource limitations (and legacy barriers) for long. All this in the context of offsite constructions where the design can directly be exported to the right CNC machines in the factory, and arranged for delivery and assembly order. We have let ourself amazed, despite the controlled demo situation and the small detail, it was a remarkable performance. For a minute or so, but thinking further, why would the customers (construction design engineers) of our competitors flow to our legacy software full of legacy pitfalls they know about and have to live with when they can turn to AI for a fresh design solution themselves, just like we did? They know the context better than us anyway, just do not have time for bit-carving. Why would we have customers when customers of our customers can turn to an AI for a design that is buildable? I was consulting one model about a structural engineering detail, and it was quite well informed I have to say. From training data alone. I felt, maybe I need to rethink the rest of my career, that is not that long but still uncomfortably long for being predictable beyond a few years. Well, things are not that bleak, probably, at least not for our customers. Regulations (accountability) and physical world matters still require them. But not us for our customers, not that much and not for too long. They tend to be the tech savvy folks eager to jump at adjacent domains when it saves them a percentage or two off the construction costs (not a small pile of money), and AI with its programming language of English and deep knowledge pool is not that big a jump from their standpoint. Our domain is pretty well formulated, regulated, documented, inherently built on do-check-adjust loops already. With a thing like AI it might worth to try making and improving a design solution in a second loop. But they also started to invest in robots already driven by software for their factories, AI might jump in there, and I wonder how much more until the regulations are forced to change by Super Intelligent (R) politicians for the sake of AI accelerated built environments (housing crisis, you know!), shifting the AI use further out towards generic population, wanting to order a new two bathroom condo for next Friday from Alibaba. The conservative construction business is a nuisance and obstacle in the way of modernisations anyway, go around it! I will go to work tomorrow, and for some time, but the picture above feel less and less fictious with each passing day of AI news and usage.

But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.

I was a game developer for many years, at large scale (MMO) and at small scale (indie). With the advent of AI, I've been _trying_ to use AI to accelerate game development and have come to a few conclusions. 1. AI models want to make everything deterministic. This sounds like a truly sound way to write a verifiable program. Games are not verifiable simulators except in the niche of ...simulators. Even in those cases, the vast infrastructure devoted to this leads to a lot of churn, bugs (AI forcing things to align with the verifier), and rigidity. 2. Making a game != Fun. This one is obvious but needs to be stated. Anyone on earth right now can say "make me doom" or "make me a super mario clone" and Opus/Astra will dutifully comply and make something generic and bland. Once the novelty of "oh wow it actually built it" wears off, you're left with a mediocre clone, lacking depth, that no customer would want hoisted upon them. 3. Content and novelty are the hard parts. AI models always create the mediocre middle. There's real work (and interesting work) involved in both inventing novel gameplay systems which LLMs will never stumble upon despite infinite 'brainstorming prompts'. But, AI is 'OK' at taking your novel idea and proposing directions -- that you can then strike down viciously until something interesting emerges. On the content side, this has always been a truism for an independent developer. AI art tools aren't quite there yet. There's image-to-3D and there's Mixamo for animation but we're not there yet. Nearly though! But again, will every game look like a bland generic AI generated image with bland AI generated models? 4. AI models are crap at building re-usable large-scale architectures. Even building with Opus 5.5 and Astra they will happy design themselves into a corner. Yes, they can _also_ design themselves out of that corner at speed - with a lot of pain and code churn and mess. I've found it vastly better to iterate slowly, using your experience (if you have it) to structure the core architecture and systems the way you want (AI writing the code) -- and then build upon that solid base -- taking special care to reject updates that butcher your architecture. I think this applies to most coding projects actually. 5. Game dev currently surfaces very clear differences in model capabilities with Opus 5.5 leading the pack (in this domain) and Fable 5.1 and Astra/GPT-6.1 Sol following a decent distance behind. Part of this is wrong usage of the tool. If you say "make a game" -- Opus will outperform the others by a large margin -- in making a generic "game" that was undefined (a paragraph of text is not a defined game). In these cases, the model has filled in all the gaps in undefined areas with average 'what probably looks good' content. You're left with something devoid of creativity. This is the problem with the myriad three.js tech demos. If you instead have a clear understanding of what you're building, models (nearly all SOTA) will get you there cheaper by building what you've asked without speculation. I don't believe you should hand off the one human worthwhile trait, creativity, to the AI -- so "Opus build a game" is indeed the wrong way. 6. It seems hard (and pointless) to collaborate with other human developers when AI coding on smaller/indie projects. Each AI model is trying to "solve the whole thing". The speed also makes it hard to stop at arbitrary boundaries and promotes a rushed feeling or conversely a sluggish feeling (AI did all the stuff, now I'm waiting to integrate with a friend/collaborator). This is probably easily solvable but has thus far felt weird when I've collaborated. 7. The return of custom engines? While models do great with Godot and Unreal, this is the chance to build custom engines like the golden years of the 2000s. OK, this one is a bit of nostalgia but I miss the world of dozen of game engines each with their own unique look and feel. Otherwise you get XBOX 360 era where every "realistic" character looks like a Gears of War meathead. Every adventure game has the same mechanics, you're hooking something, you're scooting under something, you're scooting between walls or things, you're on collapsing things that require either button sequences or hitting your 'hook' (every adventuring has some hook of infinite rope of course). OK, this entire bullet is just a rant about samey-ness. LLMs should unlock our human creativity and allow experimentation outside of that cost imposed same-ness. All things said, it's _clear_ that the acceleration is here if you know what you want. You can go from concept to prototype in a few hours. You then have to be disciplined enough to step back and rebuild that thing (with AI) correctly and towards a useful objective that you've thought up. I'm looking forward to went content creation catches up. Or perhaps that's a sad day when creativity vanishes.

Hey HN - I use quite a few coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ...) and often several of them concurrently, so it can be hard to keep track of which agent is waiting for me. So I built Muster. Press ⌥Tab and it'll show you agents that are waiting for you first, agents that are still going second, and agents that finished recently last. Release ⌥ on one, it'll bring up Claude's app, Codex's threads page, Cursor's Agents window, or the terminal that the CLI agents are running in, respectively. Agents often also require your approval for actions, have questions for you, or want you to approve plans. When one does, you get a notification at the top of your screen and can ⌥↩ / ⌥⌫ to approve/deny without disturbing what you're looking at. Press ⌃⌥Space to search across your recent (3h) agent conversations and get some stats like tokens used and estimated list price of API usage for them. MIT-licensed, requires macOS 14+, uses the native glass effects, and is a tiny AppKit app (2 MB download). In my brief (10 agents for 10 min that were all constantly updating) testing, it uses about 20 MB of memory and an average of 0.43% of a CPU core.

IMO senior software engineer is someone who drives consensus in a large organization. I dont think LLMs are going to solve that problem any time soon. I also see a bunch of skills emerging. First if you're doing frontend type dev, there is a lot of value in good aesthetics and UX intuition. You can build hundreds of prototypes and test concepts much better. On the backend, while LLMs can trace race conditions, the need to reason against spaghetti and figure out what your context window looks like is still very much there. Designing tests that ensure seamless migrations still requires a degree of human oversight. Then there are frontiers like robotics where even with LLMs coding, there are so many cross functional problems that you dont feel like you are moving faster. I work in a fairly niche role. I use llms for coding all day but there are times for the type of operations research work I do I simply find it easier to write algorithms in almost correct code.

The rate of output from LLMs is very high compared to most developers' capacity to review every line, especially when they are often working on multiple tasks from multiple projects all on the same day. The directive to increase code churning is coming from the top since upper management believes everything tech CEOs advertise to them, and there is increasing anxiety across tech, mathematics, finance, arts, etc. about getting replaced so people want to at least appear to be much more productive with AI. The new norm is fast becoming "There will be mistakes, but maybe not most of the time. We'll deal with it when we get there, and since we're all on the same boat, let's spread out the blame or try to ignore it since you never know when it might happen to you." To be fair, this was always the case as there was never any guarantee of bug-free code in general, but the difference today is mainly in volume.

It's actually worse than that. In a repo where there is a heavy amount of AI code, it becomes impossible to manually write code. The AI code favors obtuse, unmaintainable mess (from the standpoint of a non-AI dev). Constantly overwriting your changes, large comments, hacky logic, overly-defensive programming, misunderstandings that the LLM made that cause you to waste hours debugging. I've come to the realization that AI code bases are effectively AI-only code bases, unless one is using AI as just a code-autocomplete, then that seems mostly fine. But most devs are using it as an end2end implementation tool, having it 1-shot full features, and then iterating on them with the agent afterwards. The amount of churn and terrible code stops the manual coder from doing anything effectively. In my own team's codebase, I'm confident that we would actually be further along without AI, and that AI coding is a hindrance (although AI debugging seems to be a pretty good tool). It is made worse that everyone does code reviews with AI now, and it constantly gets things wrong, and when its right, it's usually for the most basic, unimportant issues (again with the overly defensive coding style). This waste the manual coder time trying to figure out if the issue its requesting a fix for is an actual problem or not.
